## ADR-017: Order Resend Delivery — same-game package swap + live price reconciliation (built 2026-07-27)

**Status:** Accepted (design) — 2026-07-27 (grilled with the founder one decision at a time, informed by direct review of the legacy KeroxShop admin's own "Resend Delivery" modal and Order Details screen — real screenshots, not recalled from memory — per this project's long-standing rule that the legacy system is UI/UX reference only, never a source of product facts, [`legacy-reference-notes.md`](./legacy-reference-notes.md))

**Context:** ORD-7's currently-shipped `retryDelivery()` (`OrderController::retryDelivery()` → `FulfillOrderJob` → `OrderFulfillmentService::fulfill()`) is a purely **idempotent resend**: it re-submits the exact same `supplier_product_ref`/`player_id`/`server_id` already snapshotted on the `Order` row, reusing the same `reference_number` (ORD-8, unchanged), and only ever runs while `delivery_status=failed`. It cannot change what's being delivered. A founder audit of the legacy KeroxShop admin's own Resend Delivery flow surfaced a materially richer feature: the admin can swap to a **different package**, sees a live price comparison against what the customer actually paid, re-validates the Player ID before resending, and the order detail page keeps a **full history** of every attempt (not just the latest). This ADR designs that richer flow for this codebase — grilled one decision at a time, since it touches money/ledger correctness (`ADR-002`), not just UI.

**Decision (per sub-area, each grilled with the founder one at a time before being accepted):**

1. **Scope: same-game package swap only.** Admin may resend against a *different* `Package`, but only one belonging to the **same `Game`** as the original order. Swapping the game itself is explicitly **deferred, not abandoned** (see decision #9) — this phase ships the lower-risk half first.
2. **Checkout snapshot stays immutable — ORD-9 is unchanged.** `Order.cost_price`/`reseller_cost_price`/`selling_price`/`final_amount`/`transaction_fee` are the historical record of what the customer was actually charged at checkout time and are **never rewritten** by a resend. A resend is a new financial event layered on top of that record, not a retroactive edit of it.
3. **Live price is a reconciliation check, not a replacement for the snapshot.** At resend time, the selected package's *current* `cost_price`/`reseller_cost_price` (already kept live by Price Sync's Price Propagation, `ADR-015`) is compared against the original order's snapshotted values, purely to answer "has this gotten more/less expensive since checkout." The platform always **absorbs** the difference in either direction — never re-charges the customer, never blocks a resend over a price increase — but "absorb" must never mean "don't record." Per the founder: failing to record a 1-sen loss is worse than the loss itself.
4. **New audit table, `order_resend_attempts` — one row per resend attempt**, mirroring this codebase's existing `price_change_logs`/`deactivation_logs` discipline (insert-only, no `updated_at`): `order_id` (cascade), `package_id` (the package actually used *this* attempt — may differ from `Order.package_id`), `cost_price_sen`/`reseller_cost_price_sen` (live values read at attempt time), `price_diff_sen` (this attempt's cost vs. the order's original snapshot), `outcome` (success/failed), `supplier_response` (raw JSON), `note` (nullable, admin's own free-text — matches the legacy modal's "Note (Optional)" field), `triggered_by` (admin, nullable). This is what the Admin Orders detail page renders as a "Delivery Logs" history table — today's schema only ever has `Order.supplier_response`, overwritten on every attempt, so no history survives past the latest try.
5. **`final_amount`/`selling_price`/`transaction_fee` stay immutable — never touched by a resend, no exception.** These are the customer-facing record of what was actually charged, and are also the source of truth for total-sales analytics/reporting — a resend, or any package swap, must never retroactively change what a sales report says the customer paid. **`platform_profit`/`reseller_profit`, by contrast, are updated at the moment delivery finally succeeds** (whichever attempt that is — original or resent) to mirror whatever was actually credited to the ledger for that order. Reasoning: `creditProfit()` only ever fires once, on the attempt that actually succeeds (no earlier attempt ever credits the ledger — confirmed in `OrderFulfillmentService::fulfill()`), so there's no double-credit risk either way — but if these two fields stayed frozen at the checkout-time estimate while a resend's `LedgerEntry` credits a *different*, recomputed figure, `Order` would permanently disagree with its own ledger entry for the same order. These fields exist to mirror the ledger, not to preserve a pre-delivery estimate — same discipline as Price Propagation updating `Package.cost_price` to live truth, applied here to `Order`'s own profit fields, with `order_resend_attempts` (#4) as the audit trail for every intermediate figure along the way. Confirmed with the founder, 2026-07-27: total-sales analytics must key off the immutable customer-charged fields above, never off profit, which is exactly why this split is safe.
6. **Player-ID re-validation is conditional on `Game.player_validator_enabled`** (the toggle already shipped in `/admin/games`, `ADR-005`'s newest addendum). If enabled, the resend flow must run a validate-ID step (reusing the existing `PlayerValidationController`/`PlayerValidator` chain) before the resend button is actionable. If the game has no validation configured, the resend proceeds directly — no new schema, this reuses an existing mechanism end to end.
7. **Supplier reference handling — no change from today's already-correct behavior.** `Order.reference_number` (ours) is reused unchanged across every resend attempt (ORD-8, unaffected by this ADR). `Order.supplier_ref` (the supplier's own returned ID) already gets overwritten to the latest value on a successful `fulfill()` call — confirmed in the current `OrderFulfillmentService::fulfill()` implementation, nothing to build here.
8. **No new `DeliveryStatus` value for a supplier-side post-success reversal ("refunded by supplier").** `delivery_status` stays binary (delivered/failed) — a supplier that reports a refund/reversal reason does so inside its own raw response body, which this codebase already stores verbatim (`Order.supplier_response`). Any "refunded (Supplier)" badge is purely a UI-level read of that existing raw field when a supplier happens to populate it — some suppliers give a reason, some don't (a bare "failed" the admin must manually confirm with the supplier directly), and that variability is inherent to the data, not something to model as a state machine.
9. **Cross-game package swap — explicitly deferred, not abandoned.** The legacy system itself never built this either; it was previously deprioritized on the reasoning that Voucher issuance already lets a customer choose a different game themselves, so an admin-side cross-game swap was judged redundant complexity for the same outcome. The founder still wants it eventually. Tracked for its own dedicated future grill session, which must cover at minimum: (a) Player-ID re-validation is **not optional** when the target game differs from the original — a validated ID for one game carries zero meaning for another, this is a different player account, not just a different SKU; (b) a package-discovery/equivalence UX across unrelated games (no schema for this exists today); (c) whether Voucher's existing self-service path still makes this not worth the complexity, or whether the founder's motivation (reducing customer friction/drop-off after a failure) justifies it anyway.

**Rationale:** Every sub-area above changes `OrderFulfillmentService`'s *implementation* around a resend, not the money-computation contracts `PricingService`/`CheckoutTotalService` already own — the same "deepen the module, don't reshape the seam" discipline this codebase has followed since `ADR-001`/`ADR-006`/`ADR-014`. Decision #3's "always absorb, always record" directly extends `ADR-002`'s ledger philosophy (full audit trail over a clean number) into a new scenario the ledger design didn't originally anticipate.

**Consequence to track:** this ADR records *design intent only* — no code exists yet, matching this project's own established practice of designing and grilling before building (`ADR-013`/`ADR-015`/`ADR-016`). All 9 decisions above are founder-confirmed, including #5's profit-field-vs-customer-charged-field split. Decision #9 (cross-game) is out of scope for whatever ships from this ADR — do not build it opportunistically alongside decisions #1–8 just because the code is nearby. Update `prd.md` §14/§15 once this actually ships.

**Addendum, 2026-07-27 (build session) — decisions #1–8 shipped, #9 still deferred:** `order_resend_attempts` (decision #4) now exists, same insert-audit discipline as `price_change_logs`/`deactivation_logs`. `OrderResendService` (`app/Services/Fulfillment/`) enforces, in order: the order is currently `delivery_status=failed` (decision #8's own state machine, unchanged — resend doesn't loosen the guard `retryDelivery()` already had), the target `Package.game_id` matches the order's own `game_id` and is active (decision #1), and — only when `Game.player_validator_enabled` and a profile is assigned — a recent `player_validations` row exists for the order's own player_id/server_id (decision #6, reusing `CheckoutController::assertPlayerIdIsValidated()`'s exact data-tuple-match discipline, not a new mechanism). `OrderController::resend()` pre-checks the same two guards synchronously for fast admin feedback, then dispatches `ResendOrderDeliveryJob` (ADR-014's async discipline — the admin panel never blocks on a live Gamevion call); the job re-derives live package values at actual attempt time and delegates to `OrderFulfillmentService::fulfill()` unchanged.

One concrete formula decision this ADR's own text left open, resolved during implementation: decision #5 says platform_profit/reseller_profit are "recomputed... to mirror whatever was actually credited," but doesn't specify the formula. Implemented by reusing `PricingService::calculate()` — the exact same function `CheckoutService::initiate()` already calls — against the *live* `cost_price`/`reseller_cost_price` of the package actually being resent, at the order's original `reseller_markup_pct`. This mirrors decision #5's own analogy ("same discipline as Price Propagation... applied here") rather than inventing a bespoke absorption formula: `Order.cost_price`/`reseller_cost_price`/`selling_price`/`final_amount`/`transaction_fee` stay exactly as decision #2 requires (never touched), while `platform_profit`/`reseller_profit` are set to this recomputed breakdown *before* `fulfill()` runs, so `creditProfit()`'s existing "fires exactly once, on success" guarantee credits the ledger with these figures — and if the attempt fails, nothing was credited, matching the checkout-time flow's own existing "stored figure is an estimate until delivery actually succeeds" behavior (not a new invariant introduced by this ADR).

Admin UI: `/admin/orders`' existing order-detail view (not a separate route) gained a "Resend Delivery…" button (gated on `delivery_status=failed`, matching the backend exactly) opening a modal — same-game active-package picker with a live cost-price reconciliation preview, an inline "Verify Player ID" step that only renders when the game requires it, and an optional note — plus a "Delivery Logs" table below the existing detail cards rendering every `order_resend_attempts` row, most recent first. 21 new backend tests (`OrderResendServiceTest` 12, `ResendOrderDeliveryJobTest` 4, `OrderControllerTest` +5 resend cases); full suite 396, all green. `npx tsc --noEmit`/`next build`/`eslint` all clean. Verified live against a real running `php artisan serve` + real Sanctum token: `GET /api/orders/{id}` returns the new `resend_attempts` relation, `POST .../resend` correctly 422s a cross-game package and 200s + queues a same-game one. **Not verified live**: an actual queued `ResendOrderDeliveryJob` run against the real Gamevion adapter — deliberately not attempted, since `GAMEVION_SANDBOX`'s real value wasn't checked first and ADR-006's own sandbox `500` limitation (or worse, an accidental real production call) makes that an action to take deliberately, not as a side effect of testing this feature. Decision #9 (cross-game swap) remains explicitly out of scope, not built.

**Addendum, 2026-07-27 (same session) — UI merged, one button instead of two:** first cut shipped "Resend Delivery…" as a *second* button next to ORD-7's original "Retry Delivery" (both gated on `delivery_status=failed`). Founder feedback: two buttons for "fix a failed delivery" was more confusing than useful — an admin shouldn't have to know in advance whether they want the plain-retry or package-swap variant before clicking. Consolidated to a single "Resend Delivery…" button whose modal **defaults the package picker to the order's own package** — submitting with no change reproduces the old "Retry Delivery" behavior exactly (the submit button itself even relabels to "Retry Delivery" when the selection is unchanged, "Resend Delivery" when it differs), routed entirely through the one resend flow (`OrderResendService`/`ResendOrderDeliveryJob`/`POST .../resend`) rather than two separate code paths. If the order's original package was deactivated since it failed (decision #1's own active-package guard would reject resubmitting to it), the modal leaves the picker empty and shows an explicit "original package no longer active — choose a replacement" notice instead of silently failing. The plain `POST /api/orders/{order}/retry-delivery` endpoint (ADR-014, `OrderController::retryDelivery()`) is unchanged and still exists on the backend — no reason to remove a working, tested primitive — it's simply no longer called from this UI; `admin/src/lib/orders.ts`'s `retryOrderDelivery()` helper was removed as genuinely dead frontend code once nothing called it. No backend logic changed, so no test/behavior impact beyond the admin UI itself.

## ADR-018: Sandbox Test Orders — a middleware-only tool for exercising the real Order lifecycle without touching real data or real money

**Status:** Accepted (design) — 2026-07-27 (grilled with the founder one decision at a time, same session as ADR-017's build; explicit founder instruction: record the full plan here for review before writing any code)

**Context:** Testing an order-lifecycle feature (Resend Delivery, order detail, Delivery Logs) today means either driving the real storefront through a real Xendit test-mode checkout every time, or creating an `Order` row by hand via `tinker` against `/admin/orders` and manually deleting it from the DB afterward once done — the exact workflow used to verify ADR-017 live this session. Founder flagged this as untenable for repeated testing and pointed to a real reference: the legacy KeroxShop admin's own middleware "Orders" page (`manage.keroxshop.com`, screenshot reviewed live) has a "Create Test Order" form and a "Test Orders" results table — but by the founder's own account, despite being labeled "test," that table is **not actually isolated** from real order data. That's the specific mistake this ADR exists to not repeat: the goal is a real, working sandbox — not a "test" label that doesn't actually mean anything downstream.

Also confirmed live (not assumed) before deciding the payment approach: fetched `docs.xendit.co/apidocs/simulate-payment-test-mode` directly — Xendit's Payment Request API v3 has no separate test host (test vs. live is purely which secret key is used) and ships an official `POST /v3/payment_requests/{id}/simulate` test-only endpoint that pushes a payment toward `SUCCEEDED` via the normal webhook. Real and useful for testing the *payment* pipeline specifically — but that pipeline is already proven live (`ADR-001`, the Payment Methods "Test" action) and is not what this sandbox exists to exercise, which is why decision #3 below skips it entirely rather than building against it.

**Decision (per sub-area, each grilled with the founder one at a time before being accepted):**

1. **Storage: reuse the real `orders` table, one new `orders.is_test` boolean column (default `false`) — not a parallel schema.** A sandbox order is a real `Order` row. This is what lets `PricingService`, `OrderResendService`, `OrderFulfillmentService`'s status-transition logic, `order_resend_attempts`, and every existing money/delivery code path run **completely unchanged** against it — the only thing that makes it "sandbox" is (a) which controller/page can reach it and (b) two narrow, explicit safety guards (decisions #5/#6). This directly targets the legacy system's actual flaw: a "test" label is worthless unless something concrete enforces exclusion downstream — here that enforcement is a hard, unconditional scope, not a flag anyone has to remember to check.
2. **UI/API placement: fully separate from `/admin/orders`, not a filter/tab inside it.** New page, `/middleware/sandbox` (naming TBD at build time), backed by a new, dedicated `Middleware\SandboxOrderController` (`index`/`store`/`show`/`resend`/`destroy`) whose every query is unconditionally scoped to `is_test = true`. `Admin\OrderController::index()`/`show()` gain a **permanent, unconditional** `where('is_test', false)` — not an admin-toggleable filter — so the real operational queue can never show sandbox data regardless of future changes to that page. Founder's own reasoning: `/admin/orders` is a money-critical tool that must be 100% trustworthy at a glance (e.g. the "Need Action" count); mixing in sandbox data — even filtered, even badged — adds a class of mistake (a filter bug, a future teammate not knowing a toggle exists) that's cheaper to eliminate structurally than to guard against per-screen. This also matches this project's own existing `/middleware` vs `/admin` split (supplier-integration/dev tooling vs. running-the-shop) — DEV-1/DEV-2's raw supplier tester already lives in `/middleware` for the same reason.
3. **Creation skips Xendit entirely — `payment_status` is set to `paid` immediately, no payment call of any kind.** Admin picks a real `Game`/`Package` from our own catalog (via the existing `GET /api/games`/`GET /api/games/{game}/packages` admin endpoints — not raw supplier fields typed by hand, unlike legacy's page) so `PricingService` computes real, consistent money figures. Player ID/Server ID and customer email/name are editable but default to fixed sandbox placeholders. Rejected alternative: Xendit's own `/simulate` endpoint (confirmed to exist, see Context) — not used, since it would add an async payment_status=pending wait for a pipeline already proven live elsewhere, for zero benefit to what this tool actually needs to prove.
4. **Sandbox orders are created directly at `delivery_status = failed`** (skipping `not_started`/`processing`) — framed as "pretend a first delivery attempt already happened and failed." This is deliberate, not an oversight: it's the exact state `OrderResendService`'s existing guard requires before a resend is actionable, so a freshly created sandbox order is immediately usable with the real, unmodified Resend Delivery UI — no separate "first delivery" affordance needs to be built.
5. **Delivery never calls the real `GamevionAdapter` — a new `FakeSupplierAdapter` (`App\Services\Supplier\`, implements the existing `SupplierAdapter` interface) is used instead, swapped in by construction, not by branching inside the fulfillment/resend services.** `Middleware\SandboxOrderController::resend()` builds its own `OrderResendService`/`OrderFulfillmentService` instance directly (constructor-injecting `FakeSupplierAdapter`) rather than resolving `SupplierAdapter` through the container's default binding (which stays `GamevionAdapter`, untouched, for the real `Admin\OrderController` path) — the same substitution the Adapter pattern (`ADR-006`) exists to make cheap. Runs **synchronously, inline, no queue dispatch** — `ResendOrderDeliveryJob`/`FulfillOrderJob` are not involved at all for sandbox orders, since there's no real network latency to hide from the admin request, and it means a sandbox order never depends on a queue worker actually running (a real, documented gotcha that already bit a live session this week per `prd.md`'s Price Sync founder-testing note). The admin chooses the simulated outcome (success, or failure with a canned error code/message) each time via an extra control in the reused Resend Delivery modal, visible only in the sandbox context — a fake adapter that only ever "succeeds" would make it impossible to test the exact `need_action` → `Resend Delivery` → outcome loop this tool exists to exercise.
6. **One new, narrow guard in existing fulfillment code — the only touch to money-critical logic this ADR makes:** `OrderFulfillmentService::creditProfit()` gets `if ($order->is_test) { return; }` before it writes any `LedgerEntry`. This is deliberately the single, explicit, easy-to-audit place a sandbox order is stopped from ever reaching the real ledger — chosen over a parallel "sandbox fulfillment service" specifically so the real status-transition/reference-number logic stays 100% shared and unduplicated between real and test orders (only the money-writing tail end is skipped), and chosen over swapping `LedgerService` itself (a `final` class, not behind an interface — substituting it would be a much larger change for the same guarantee).
7. **Cleanup is a real delete action in the sandbox page itself** (single row, and a "Delete All Test Orders" bulk action) — hard-deletes the `Order` row; `order_resend_attempts` cascade-deletes with it (existing FK). Safe with no residue precisely because of decision #6: a sandbox order, by construction, never had a real `LedgerEntry` to leave behind.
8. **Frontend: extract, don't duplicate.** The order-detail cards, the Resend Delivery modal, and the Delivery Logs table (already built for `/admin/orders`, ADR-017) are pulled into shared components consumed by **both** `/admin/orders` and the new `/middleware/sandbox` page, each against its own backend endpoint (`Admin\OrderController` vs. `Middleware\SandboxOrderController`). This is what actually delivers the founder's stated goal — "output yang sama macam workflow production" — without the two pages' behavior silently drifting apart over time the way two independently-maintained UIs would.

**Rationale:** Every decision above keeps `PricingService`, `OrderStatusService`, `OrderResendService`'s validation logic, and the `order_resend_attempts` audit trail completely unchanged and shared — the only new, sandbox-specific code is the `is_test` scope, the `FakeSupplierAdapter`, one guard line in `creditProfit()`, and the dedicated controller/page. This is the same "deepen the module, don't reshape the seam" discipline `ADR-001`/`ADR-006`/`ADR-014`/`ADR-017` already established, applied to a testing concern instead of a business feature — and it's the concrete difference between this design and the legacy page it was prompted by: isolation enforced at the query/ledger boundary, not left as an unenforced label.

**Consequence to track:** this ADR records *design intent only* — no code exists yet, matching this project's own established practice (`ADR-013`/`ADR-015`/`ADR-016`/`ADR-017`). Update `prd.md` §14/§15 once this actually ships. Decision #5's exact `FakeSupplierAdapter` outcome-picker UI and decision #8's exact shared-component boundaries are implementation details to finalize during the build session, not decisions still open — the founder-facing behavior (mock delivery, admin picks the outcome, fully separate page, real delete) is what's confirmed here.

**Addendum — shipped, 2026-07-30/31 (build session, same day as the founder's 2026-07-30 pointer marking this item 1 of the next-session order) — every decision above built exactly as designed, no deviations:** `orders.is_test` (boolean, default `false`) added via migration; `Order::$fillable`/`$casts` updated. `App\Services\Supplier\FakeSupplierAdapter` implements `SupplierAdapter` with zero network calls — `createOrder()` branches on a constructor-supplied `simulateSuccess` flag, returning a canned `SANDBOX-*` supplier_ref on success or the admin's chosen error_code/error_message on failure; `validatePlayer()` throws `ValidationNotSupportedException` (sandbox orders never validate against a real supplier). `Middleware\SandboxOrderController` (index/store/show/resend/destroy/destroyAll), every query unconditionally scoped `is_test = true`; route-model-bound actions (`show`/`resend`/`destroy`) additionally `abort(404)` if the resolved Order isn't a sandbox row, since binding alone only knows the primary key. `store()` mirrors `CheckoutController`'s own game/package/reseller resolution (`Reseller::platformOwner()`, `PricingService::calculate()`) but skips Xendit entirely and creates directly at `payment_status=paid`/`delivery_status=failed`. `resend()` builds `OrderFulfillmentService`/`OrderResendService` via `new` (not container resolution), constructor-injecting `FakeSupplierAdapter` — confirmed live that this correctly bypasses the container's real `GamevionAdapter`/`CircuitBreakingSupplierAdapter` binding entirely, synchronously, no queue. `OrderFulfillmentService::creditProfit()` gained the one-line `is_test` guard (decision #6). `Admin\OrderController::index()`/`show()` gained the permanent `where('is_test', false)`/`abort(404)` scope (decision #2) — and, found only while implementing (not in the original decision list, but directly implied by it): the same guard was added to `retryDelivery()`/`resend()` too, since a sandbox order id could otherwise reach the real, queued `GamevionAdapter` path via those two endpoints despite never being visible through `index()`/`show()` — closing a real isolation gap decision #2's original wording didn't explicitly call out.

Frontend (decision #8): `OrderDetailCards`/`DeliveryLogsTable` extracted from `/admin/orders`'s page component into `admin/src/components/orders/`, now consumed by both `/admin/orders` and the new `/middleware/sandbox` page unchanged. `ResendDeliveryModal` gained an optional `sandbox` prop — when set, renders a "Simulated Outcome" success/failure toggle (plus optional error code/message fields on failure) and posts to the sandbox endpoint instead of the real one; every other field (package picker, live cost reconciliation, player-ID re-validation gate) behaves identically in both contexts, confirmed live: a sandbox order against a game with `player_validator_enabled` correctly rejected the resend with the same "Please re-validate this Player ID" message the real flow gives, since `OrderResendService`'s validation logic runs completely unchanged. New `CreateSandboxOrderModal` (game/package pickers via the existing `lib/games.ts`, not shared with `/admin/orders` since real orders have no equivalent admin-creation flow). New `/middleware/sandbox` page + `lib/sandboxOrders.ts` API client; new "Sandbox" nav entry in the Middleware Panel layout.

19 new backend tests (`SandboxOrderControllerTest` 14, `OrderFulfillmentServiceTest` +1 is_test-guard case, `Admin\OrderControllerTest` +4 sandbox-exclusion cases); full backend suite **483/483 green**. `npx tsc --noEmit`/`next build` clean on `admin/`. Verified live end-to-end, twice — once via direct API calls against the real local Herd backend (create → resend-success → resend-failure → delete, confirming zero `LedgerEntry` rows and a real `404` from every `Admin\OrderController` action against the sandbox order id), once through the actual browser UI (create a test order via the modal, resend with a simulated failure showing the typed error code/message in Supplier response, resend again with simulated success reaching `delivered` with a `SANDBOX-*` supplier_ref and the Resend Delivery button correctly disappearing once no longer resendable, Delivery Logs showing both attempts with the real admin's name, delete, and confirmed `/admin/orders` shows only real orders throughout).

## ADR-019: Second-pass resilience & security audit — reconciling ADR-014 against real code, docs restructure

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-27 (findings and sequencing discussed with the founder in a dedicated audit session; grilled on the "fix now vs. wait for deploy" split specifically, not per-item)

**Context:** ADR-014 (2026-07-26) recorded a 24/7 burst-resilience baseline — queue, retry, indexing, caching, rate-limiting, observability — as design intent, later confirmed built the same day (`prd.md` §14, 2026-07-26 entry). A full read-only re-audit was run 2026-07-27 (four scoped reviews: DB indexing + caching, queue/retry/load-balancing, observability, and OWASP-adjacent security — mass assignment, validation, CSRF, XSS, SQL injection) to verify ADR-014 against the actual code rather than trust the design doc, and to check the security surface ADR-014 didn't scope at all.

Result: all six of ADR-014's decisions are genuinely shipped as designed. Two things that looked like gaps on first read are not — they're the founder's own already-recorded deferrals: Redis (ADR-014 decision #1, deferred until real traffic justifies the infra) and Sentry/external error-tracking (ADR-014 decision #6, explicitly declined for cost/data-residency before real production traffic exists). What the audit did find genuinely new: a handful of code-level gaps ADR-014 never scoped (mostly on the auth/payment edges), one correction to an existing docs claim, and a confirmation that the project's production-infra gap (no queue worker, no Redis/S3 provisioned anywhere — `docker-compose.yml` still defines MySQL only) is real and unaddressed, consistent with `prd.md`'s own repeated note that this project is still 100% local Herd, no production host chosen (ADR-010).

**Decision — sequenced by what's actionable now vs. genuinely blocked on a production-host decision, not by raw severity:**

1. **Fix now — pure code/migration, no infra dependency, testable on local Herd:**
   - Add an index on `orders.created_at` (the default, unfiltered Admin Orders listing sorts by it with nothing backing that sort) and replace the "today" filter's `whereDate('created_at', ...)` with `whereBetween()` — `whereDate()` wraps the column in a function, which defeats any index on it regardless.
   - Verify the 7 tables using `foreignId()->constrained()` without a confirmed standalone index (`player_region_mappings`, `player_validations`, `price_change_logs`, `deactivation_logs`, `order_resend_attempts`, `games.player_validator_profile_id`, `gallery_images.uploaded_by`) via `SHOW INDEX` against real MySQL — the same gotcha already hit and fixed once, on `packages.supplier_id` (see ADR-006's neighboring migration note).
   - Add an idempotency key to `XenditGateway::createPayment()` — the shared `TransientFailureRetryPolicy` (ADR-014 #2) can retry a request that Xendit actually processed but whose response was lost, creating a second live payment request for the same order. This is a real double-charge risk distinct from order-fulfillment idempotency (PAY-2), which is already handled.
   - Add the same explicit short HTTP timeout to `XenditGateway::client()` that `GamevionAdapter` already has (with its own documented reasoning) — without it, a slow Xendit response can hold a request thread for the HTTP client's much longer default, compounded across retry attempts, on what is a customer-facing checkout path.
   - Log checkout failures (`CheckoutController`'s `catch (CheckoutFailedException $e)`, currently silent — no record anywhere of *why* a checkout failed) and admin login attempts, success and failure (`AuthController::login()`, currently unlogged — no audit trail for a brute-force attempt or a compromised account).
   - Rate-limit `POST /api/login` — the only mutating auth-adjacent route with no `throttle`, unlike `/checkout` (ADR-014 #4) and `/validate-player`.
   - Decide and either enforce or explicitly descope the existing `mfa_secret`/`mfa_enabled` columns on `AdminUser` — the schema exists (added ahead of this feature being built) but `AuthController::login()` never checks either, despite `foundation-security.md` mandating MFA ahead of withdrawal/voucher actions.
   - Fix `Admin\GalleryImageController` to read the upload disk from config (`FILESYSTEM_DISK`) instead of the hardcoded `'public'` string. This corrects `prd.md` §15's Image Gallery note ("a later swap to a real bucket costs a disk-config change, not a rewrite") — that's only true once this lands; today the disk is hardcoded, so an env-only swap wouldn't actually take effect.
2. **Defer until a production host is chosen — Redis/S3/worker specifics genuinely depend on the target, config now would be guesswork:**
   - Provision a real queue-worker process. `docker-compose.yml` defines `mysql` only — no worker container, no app container at all. This isn't hypothetical: the founder's own 2026-07-27 live-testing pass (`prd.md` §14) already hit the local-equivalent of this exact gap — Herd doesn't run a worker on its own either.
   - Move `CACHE_STORE`/`QUEUE_CONNECTION` off `database` to Redis once there's ops budget for the extra infra — reaffirming, not overriding, ADR-014 decision #1's own deferral reasoning.
   - Move gallery/hero-slide uploads to the already-configured (but unused) `s3` filesystem disk once a bucket exists — blocked on item 1's disk-config fix first.
   - Wire centralized log shipping — a Papertrail-shaped channel template already exists in `config/logging.php`, unused — once there's a production target to ship to.
3. **Revisit once there's real production traffic to learn from:**
   - Thread a request-correlation ID from inbound HTTP requests into the jobs they dispatch (each job already logs with good internal context via `Log::withContext()`; there's just no link from "this customer's request" to "the job it triggered" today).
   - Basic metrics — queue depth, job failure rate, checkout error rate. Extend `HealthController` with a threshold check first; a full metrics exporter is a later, bigger lift.
   - Schedule the existing `Smoke\{Xendit,Gamevion}SmokeTest` console commands as synthetic monitoring instead of leaving them dev/manual-only.
   - Add client-side error tracking to `admin/` and `storefront/` (neither has an `error.tsx` boundary or a reporting client today — a crashed component or failed fetch on the storefront is currently invisible until a customer complains).
   - FRAUD-1..4 (blacklist) — already tracked "Not started" in `prd.md` §15, reaffirmed here as a real, stated requirement in `foundation-security.md` with zero implementation, not a silent gap.
   - The small `lockForUpdate()` gap in `Admin\WithdrawalController::reject()`/`complete()` (unlike `approve()`, which already locks) — an audit-trail race only, no double financial movement, since the ledger is only touched in `approve()`.
4. **Docs restructure, done alongside this ADR:** root `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` were auto-generated multi-agent-swarm tooling boilerplate with zero project-specific content — confirmed unused in practice (this audit session used none of it). Replaced with project-specific orientation (stack, layout, working conventions, ADR-driven-decision discipline) in `AGENTS.md`, with `CLAUDE.md` now a one-line `@AGENTS.md` import, matching the pattern `admin/`/`storefront/` already used. Added `backend/CLAUDE.md` (Laravel-specific conventions, loaded only when working in `backend/`, per how nested `CLAUDE.md` files are actually resolved) and a root `README.md` for onboarding/handoff. `mattpocock-skills` (grilling, codebase-design, domain-modeling) are named explicitly in `AGENTS.md` as the project's house style, since their vocabulary was already showing up unattributed in this very ADR log (`ADR-014`'s "each grilled with the founder," this doc's repeated "deepen the module, don't reshape the seam") — making the practice explicit rather than leaving it implicit.

**Rationale:** Same interface-vs-implementation discipline as every prior resilience/security ADR — nothing in Decision-1 or Decision-2 changes a public contract (`PaymentGateway`, `SupplierAdapter`, `OrderFulfillmentService` are all untouched). Sequencing by deploy-dependency rather than raw severity matches this project's actual state: the code-level fixes cost nothing to do now and mean deploy day is infra wiring only, not a second security pass rushed under launch pressure; the infra-dependent items would just be guesswork before a host is chosen, and revisiting them then is not a delay, it's the correct order of operations.

**Consequence to track:** update `prd.md` §14/§15 as each Decision-1 item ships — this is exactly the kind of finding `AGENTS.md`'s new "keep §14/§15 current" convention exists for. Decisions 2 and 3 are sequencing intent, not scope reduction — each has an explicit trigger condition (production host chosen / real traffic exists) to re-open it; don't let "deferred" quietly become "forgotten." The full findings detail (file:line-level, all four scoped reviews) lives in the audit session transcript, not duplicated here — this entry records the decisions made from it, per this doc's own established convention (see ADR-014's Context for the same choice).

**Addendum — self-review before committing this session's docs changes, 2026-07-27 (same session, not a new audit round):**

1. **Missed finding: per-supplier circuit breaker.** `foundation-security.md` §6 and `prd.md` (DASH-2, §9 Non-Functional Requirements) both state this as an explicit **MVP** requirement — unchecked in the checklist, not implemented in code, and this ADR's Decision-1/2/3 lists above do not cover it. What exists today (`TransientFailureRetryPolicy`) is a different mechanism: it retries *within* one request; a circuit breaker trips *across* requests after repeated failures and stops attempting calls to a down supplier for a cooldown window, preventing a retry storm across many concurrent orders when a supplier has a sustained outage. This is pure code with no infra dependency (belongs conceptually with Decision-1), but is a larger unit of work than that list's other items (a new stateful component, not a one-line fix or single migration) — recorded here as its own explicitly tracked item rather than silently folded into either list: **build a `SupplierCircuitBreaker` (or equivalent) wrapping the `GamevionAdapter`/`XenditGateway` call sites, before treating ADR-019's fix-now list as complete.**
2. **This entry's own "Accepted" status overstated how thoroughly the individual decisions were reviewed.** Unlike ADR-014/015/016/017/018, each of which records being "grilled with the founder one at a time," this session grilled the *fix-now vs. defer-until-host vs. defer-until-traffic sequencing* as one decision, not each of the roughly fifteen individual findings one by one. Recorded here rather than silently edited into the Status line above, per this project's own no-silent-rewrite convention (`foundation-security.md`'s own stated rule for itself, applied here to this doc too).

**Consequence to track:** the circuit breaker item is not yet reflected in `prd.md` §14/§15 — add it once built, same as any other Decision-1 item.

**See ADR-041** for the checkout-level idempotency key design (originally this entry's Addendum, 2026-07-29) — moved out to its own entry since it's an ADR-scale decision (new column, new exception type, three-way branch in `CheckoutController::store()`) bolted on as an addendum, not a small refinement of this ADR's fix-now list.

**Addendum — fix-now list shipped, 2026-07-29 (new session, read-only audit converted into an implementation pass at the founder's direction):** every Decision-1 item is now built and tested (416 tests passing on the fast suite, 4 on the concurrency suite against real MySQL), except MFA, which the founder explicitly chose to descope rather than build this session (see its own line below). What shipped:
- `orders.created_at` index + `OrderController`'s `today` filter switched from `whereDate()` to `whereBetween()` (the former defeats any index on the column regardless of whether one exists).
- The 7 tables flagged as "unverified FK indexes" were checked directly against real MySQL (`SHOW INDEX FROM`, per `backend/CLAUDE.md`'s own standing instruction) and all 7 already had one — `foreignId()->constrained()` does reliably index itself on this schema. **What that verification pass found instead, previously unknown:** two migrations (`player_region_mappings`'s `unique(['player_validator_profile_id','country_code'])`, `player_validations`'s 4-column `index([...])`) have Laravel-auto-generated index names exceeding MySQL's 64-character identifier limit — `php artisan migrate:fresh` against real MySQL failed outright on both, a bug sqlite's default test suite can never surface (no such limit). Both fixed with explicit short names. This is a genuine, previously-undetected production-deploy blocker directly relevant to ADR-020 (real MySQL, not sqlite) — worth a full migration-file sweep for the same pattern before the first production deploy, not assumed fixed just because these two are.
- `XenditGateway`: explicit HTTP timeout (10s/5s, config-driven, mirrors `GamevionAdapter`'s own pattern) — the actual idempotency-key research (below) landed here too, as a doc comment on `CheckoutService::initiate()`'s `createPayment()` call.
- **Idempotency-key research, verified directly against docs.xendit.co (not assumed):** Xendit's Payment Request v3 API has **no client-supplied idempotency-key header** — its OpenAPI spec documents exactly 3 request headers (`api-version`/`for-user-id`/`with-split-rule`), none of them idempotency-related. Its real dedupe mechanism is server-side `reference_id` uniqueness: a second `POST` with the same `reference_id` (this codebase already sends `order.order_number`, stable per Order) gets a clean `409 DATA_NOT_FOUND` "Duplication is not allowed," never a second live payment request. This means a `TransientFailureRetryPolicy` retry *within* one `createPayment()` call was already safe against double-charging before this session — the real, still-open gap is different from what this ADR's fix-now list assumed: a **retried `POST /api/checkout` HTTP request** (customer double-click, client-side timeout retry) calls `CheckoutService::initiate()` again from scratch with a **brand-new** `order_number` each time, which Xendit's `reference_id` check can't catch at all. Closing that needs a client-supplied checkout-level idempotency key — a request-contract change touching `storefront/` too, not built this session (flagged, not silently dropped — see `prd.md` §14's newest NEXT SESSION pointer).
- `AuthController::login()` and `CheckoutController`'s `CheckoutFailedException` catch now log every attempt/failure (`Log::info`/`Log::warning`, admin_id/email/ip for login, game_id/package_id/channel_code for checkout — never a password or full customer PII).
- `POST /api/login` now rate-limited (`throttle:5,1` — tighter than checkout/validate-player's `10,1`, since this is a brute-force target, not a genuine-retry-tolerant customer action).
- **MFA — explicitly descoped, founder decision, 2026-07-29:** `mfa_secret`/`mfa_enabled` columns remain unchecked by `AuthController::login()`. Founder chose not to build the full TOTP enrollment+verify flow this session (a real feature — QR-secret generation, verify-and-enable endpoint, login-time code check, recovery codes, plus `admin/` UI — not a one-line patch). Recorded here per this doc's own no-silently-forgotten discipline: still a real, stated `foundation-security.md` §1 requirement, zero implementation, deliberately deferred rather than built partially or assumed done.
- `Admin\GalleryImageController`'s disk moved off the hardcoded `'public'` string. **Not** wired to the app-wide `FILESYSTEM_DISK`/`filesystems.default` — that env is already set to `local` in this project's own `.env` for unrelated reasons, and reusing it would have silently broken gallery's public-URL requirement (`local` has none). Given its own dedicated `filesystems.gallery_disk` (`GALLERY_DISK` env, defaults `public`) instead — corrects `prd.md` §15's Image Gallery note, which assumed the app-wide disk setting was the right lever.
- **`SupplierCircuitBreaker` built** — `App\Services\CircuitBreaker\CircuitBreaker` (cache-backed via the `database` store per ADR-014, so state is visible across queue-worker processes; simplified two-state closed/open, not a textbook three-state breaker — see its own doc comment for why that's an acceptable trade for this system's actual concurrency profile) wrapping `GamevionAdapter` via a new `App\Services\Supplier\CircuitBreakingSupplierAdapter` decorator (ADAPT-3: any future second `SupplierAdapter` gets the same protection just by being wrapped the same way, no interface change). **One correctness fix beyond the ADR's original one-line description:** the breaker only trips on `SupplierResponse::isServerError` (a new field, HTTP 5xx) — an ordinary 4xx business rejection (invalid product, insufficient balance) now resets the failure count as a health signal instead of counting toward tripping. Without this split, three unrelated "insufficient balance" orders in a row would have wrongly blocked every other order/game on a perfectly healthy supplier — the literal wording in this ADR's addendum above didn't anticipate that distinction, but `foundation-security.md` §6's actual requirement ("a down supplier must not be able to cascade into blocking the whole delivery queue") implies it. Deliberately scoped to suppliers only (not `XenditGateway`, despite this ADR's addendum text naming both) — `foundation-security.md` §6 and DASH-2 both scope the *stated* MVP requirement to per-supplier only; `CircuitBreaker` itself is generic enough to wrap `XenditGateway` later if that's ever decided, without rework. ~~No dashboard UI yet (`CircuitBreaker::state()` exists for whenever DASH-2's Dashboard screen gets built — still "Not started" per `prd.md` §15).~~ **Dashboard screen built 2026-08-27 — see [ADR-045](./adr.md), `CircuitBreaker::state()` now wired to `/admin`'s System Health section.**

## ADR-020: Production host — DigitalOcean Basic Droplet + Managed MySQL, Docker Compose, Cloudflare-fronted (Phase 1 built 2026-07-30 — droplet purchase + SSH-deploy still outstanding, see addendum)

**Status:** Accepted (design) — 2026-07-29 (grilled with the founder one decision at a time via `/mattpocock-skills:grilling`, against the founder's own prior research — a DigitalOcean pricing-calculator screenshot and a hand-drawn architecture diagram — same discipline as ADR-014 through ADR-019; explicit founder instruction: draft the full ADR now, build happens in a new session)

**Context:** Every prior ADR that touched production infrastructure (`ADR-015` decision #6, `ADR-016`, `ADR-019` decision #2) recorded the same genuine blocker: no production host had been chosen, so Redis/S3/queue-worker/log-shipping specifics would have been guesswork. This ADR resolves that blocker. The founder had already researched a concrete shape before this session — a single DigitalOcean Droplet running Laravel, both Next.js apps, MySQL, Redis, a queue worker, and a backup script, plus DigitalOcean Spaces for media and private MySQL backups — priced against DigitalOcean's own calculator (Basic Droplet, Regular CPU, 8 GiB/4 vCPU/160 GiB SSD/5,000 GiB transfer, $48/mo, with the "Enable backups" add-on checked, daily/7-30-day retention).

**One founder-stated priority governs every decision below, and reverses a default assumption several earlier ADRs made under a different constraint:** cost is explicitly *not* the optimization target. The founder's own words: money spent to keep the system from crashing, easy to maintain, and scalable for traffic that may exceed what's typical for a Malaysia-only top-up store — including a real plan to expand beyond Malaysia — is money the founder is willing to spend. This is the opposite starting position from, e.g., `ADR-001`'s "no second gateway is confirmed, building one now would be guessing" caution or `ADR-015`'s cost-conscious scoping — those were right for their own context (unconfirmed future need), but production infrastructure now has a confirmed, present need (a real host is being provisioned this session), so several sub-decisions below deliberately spend more than the founder's own initial research proposed, where a stronger reliability/scalability case existed.

**Decision (per sub-area, each grilled with the founder one at a time before being accepted):**

1. **Compute — one DigitalOcean Basic Droplet, 8 GiB RAM / 4 vCPU / 160 GiB SSD, Singapore region, with DigitalOcean's own Droplet Backups add-on enabled (daily, 7–30 day retention).** One droplet, one region, for now — a second droplet, a second region, and a DigitalOcean Load Balancer ($12/mo minimum) are **explicitly deferred, not provisioned speculatively**, despite the founder's stated appetite for spending on reliability. Rationale for deferring specifically this item, grilled and confirmed: the system has **zero production traffic today** (checkout is still sandbox-only per `prd.md` §14) — provisioning multi-region/load-balanced infrastructure now would be a different flavor of the same mistake `ADR-015`/`ADR-016` were built to avoid (designing against a shape with no real signal yet), not a cost-saving compromise. The trigger to revisit is concrete, not vague: sustained high CPU/RAM on this droplet, or a confirmed launch date for a second country. Droplet Backups (whole-disk snapshot) is deliberately **separate from, and complementary to**, the DB-level backup mechanism in Decision 2 — one recovers the whole box, the other recovers just the database from an independent, queryable source.
2. **Database — DigitalOcean Managed MySQL, not self-hosted on the droplet.** This reverses the founder's own initial research (which had MySQL living on the same droplet as everything else). Starter tier confirmed against DigitalOcean's own pricing page: 2 GiB RAM / 1 vCPU / 30–60 GiB storage, $30.45/mo, upgradeable to a standby node (automatic failover) once justified. **Rationale, grilled specifically against the founder's "don't fear cost" instruction:** `orders`, `ledger_entries`, `withdrawals`, and `vouchers` are the platform's money-critical tables (`backend/CLAUDE.md`'s own stated invariants). Self-hosted MySQL on the same droplet as the app means a droplet-level fault (OOM kill from the Next.js/PHP-FPM processes sharing the box, kernel panic, disk exhaustion) takes the database down with everything else, and recovery means restoring from the last `mysqldump` — losing every transaction between that dump and the crash. Managed MySQL's optional standby-node failover closes exactly this gap (automatic switch in seconds, not a restore-and-lose-data event), and DigitalOcean handles patching/point-in-time recovery instead of the founder. This is the single highest-value place to spend beyond the founder's own original research, given the explicit no-crash priority.
3. **Cache — Redis, self-hosted in a Docker container on the droplet, cache-only.** Redis is **not** used as the queue driver — the queue stays on the `database` driver (`ADR-014` decision #1's original choice), now backed by Managed MySQL. **This decision explicitly supersedes `ADR-014` decision #1's Redis deferral** (per this doc's own no-silent-rewrite convention — recorded as a new entry, not an edit to that one): Redis is being provisioned from day one of production, reversing "deferred until real traffic justifies it." What does *not* change is the reasoning for why self-hosted (not Managed Redis/Valkey, $15/mo+) is still correct here, even under a spend-for-reliability mandate: everything Redis holds in this system is regenerable cache (`Games`/`Packages`/`Payment Methods` listings, 60s TTL, per `ADR-014` decision #5) — a crash loses nothing that a fresh read from Managed MySQL can't immediately replace. Spending on managed HA for data that carries zero loss-of-data risk would be spending on the wrong thing. **Explicit revisit triggers** (so "self-hosted for now" doesn't quietly become "self-hosted forever" without anyone noticing the context changed): (a) the queue driver ever moves off `database` onto Redis — at that point Redis starts holding money-relevant, non-regenerable job state, changing this calculus entirely; (b) Redis downtime is observed to visibly degrade the customer-facing checkout path; (c) a second droplet/region (Decision 1's deferred trigger) needs a Redis instance shared across boxes, which self-hosted-per-droplet can't do.
4. **Containerization — Docker Compose, not a native LEMP-style install directly on the droplet's OS.** Chosen specifically because the founder's stated priority is ease of horizontal scaling and eventual multi-country expansion, not minimizing today's RAM footprint on one box — a reversal of this assistant's own initial lean toward native, revised once that priority was made explicit. This does **not** reopen `ADR-010` (Docker for MySQL-only, no full Sail stack) — that decision was scoped to *local development*, where Herd already worked and full containerization added no benefit; this decision is scoped to *production*, a materially different context (multi-box scaling, reproducible deploys, CI/CD image pipelines are real needs there that don't exist for one developer's local machine).
5. **Process supervision — Docker-native (`restart: unless-stopped`) plus Laravel's own `--max-jobs`/`--max-time` worker-recycling flags. No Supervisor.** Queue workers are split into separate named Docker Compose services by queue (e.g. `queue-worker-orders`, `queue-worker-pricesync`), not one worker consuming every queue — so a slow, non-urgent `SyncSupplierPricesJob` run can never head-of-line-block an urgent, money-touching `FulfillOrderJob`. **Rationale:** Supervisor's three real jobs — auto-restart on crash, N-way concurrent workers, and managing several distinct worker programs from one tool — are each already covered natively once Docker is the runtime (restart policy, `--scale`, and multiple Compose services, respectively). Supervisor is the correct, arguably only, choice on a bare VPS with no container runtime (which is why most Laravel deployment tutorials and Laravel Forge itself default to it) — but nesting Supervisor inside a container on top of Docker's own restart policy stacks two process managers solving the identical problem, for this codebase's actual (containerized) deployment shape.
6. **Load balancing / multi-region — deferred (see Decision 1), but the chosen shape is already positioned for it.** Docker images, Managed MySQL external to any one droplet, and DigitalOcean Spaces for all file storage mean the application layer holds no droplet-local state that would block adding a second droplet — the same "already positioned for it" discipline `ADR-014` decision #7 recorded for load balancing generally, now concretely true for this system: a second droplet/region is "add capacity," not "redesign for statelessness first."
7. **Network/security — DigitalOcean Cloud Firewall restricting inbound to 80/443/22 only.** MySQL is off-box entirely (Decision 2); Redis never needs a public port, only Docker's internal network. SSH is hardened to **key-only auth + `fail2ban`** — a non-standard SSH port was considered and rejected (grilled explicitly): it's security-through-obscurity, not real additional protection, and costs real operational friction (remembering a non-default port) for no measurable safety gain.
8. **Domain/DNS/SSL — DNS stays at Cloudflare (the founder's existing domain registrar), not migrated to DigitalOcean's DNS.** Cloudflare Proxy ("orange cloud") is enabled, giving free DDoS protection, edge CDN caching, and origin-IP concealment — the CDN caching in particular directly serves the founder's stated international-expansion plan, since Cloudflare's edge network serves static assets from a point of presence closer to a non-Malaysia customer than a single Singapore droplet ever could alone. SSL is terminated via a **Cloudflare Origin CA certificate** installed on the droplet's Nginx (15-year validity — no Let's Encrypt renewal cron needed at all, simpler than this assistant's original suggestion), Cloudflare's own SSL mode set to **Full (Strict)**. A DigitalOcean **Reserved IP** is attached to the droplet, and Cloudflare's DNS A record points at that Reserved IP, not the droplet's own ephemeral IP — a future droplet rebuild/resize only requires re-attaching the Reserved IP, never touching DNS.
9. **CI/CD — GitHub Actions, two phases, fully automated (no manual approval gate).** Confirmed by inspection, not assumed, before deciding: this repo has **zero CI/CD and zero E2E test infrastructure today** (`.github/` doesn't exist; no Playwright anywhere in `admin/`/`storefront/`).
   - **Phase 1 (build now, this session or the next):** backend fast test suite (sqlite) → backend concurrency suite (`phpunit.concurrency.xml`, against a MySQL service container inside the Actions runner itself, not the production Managed DB) → admin/storefront `tsc --noEmit` / `next build` / `eslint` → build three Docker images (backend, storefront, admin — queue workers reuse the backend image with a different command) → push to DigitalOcean Container Registry (Basic tier, $5/mo, 5 repos/5 GiB, confirmed sufficient) → SSH deploy (`docker compose pull && up -d`, then `php artisan migrate`) → a post-deploy `GET /api/health` check with automatic rollback to the previous image tag on failure. Deliberately **no manual approval click** — the safety net is the test stages themselves, which are already strong (396+ backend tests including the concurrency proofs on `Ledger`/`Voucher`/`OrderFulfillmentService`), not a human glancing at a button before deploying.
   - **Phase 2 (decision recorded now, build explicitly deferred, not abandoned — matching this doc's own established pattern, e.g. `ADR-017` decision #9):** Playwright E2E covering the golden paths — guest checkout → payment → order status; admin login → view order → Resend Delivery. Not required to gate the first production deploy (Phase 1's existing test gate is already strong), but tracked as the **immediate next priority** once this ADR itself is settled, given this is a money-moving system with currently zero UI-level regression coverage.
10. **Build sequencing — everything except the final SSH-deploy step can be built and proven before the droplet is purchased.** Dockerfiles, `docker-compose.yml`, and every GitHub Actions stage up through pushing images to the Container Registry depend on nothing that requires real infrastructure to exist yet — they can be built and validated now (a local Docker Compose stack, a CI-only MySQL service container). Only the SSH-deploy step needs a real target (droplet IP, SSH key). Building the rest now means the first real production deploy of a money-critical system is "run an already-proven pipeline against a new target," not "build and debug the pipeline for the first time under launch pressure."

**Rationale:** Every decision above traces back to the founder's single explicit governing priority for this ADR — reliability/no-crash and future scalability outrank minimizing spend — and each sub-decision was grilled individually against that priority rather than assumed to follow automatically from it (Decision 1's single-droplet-for-now and Decision 3's self-hosted-Redis are both deliberate *exceptions* to "spend more," grilled and justified on their own terms: no signal yet, and zero data-loss risk, respectively — spending for reliability everywhere indiscriminately would itself be a mistake, just the opposite one from under-spending).

**Consequence to track:** this ADR records *design intent only* — nothing here is built, purchased, or provisioned yet (matching `ADR-015`/`ADR-016`/`ADR-017`/`ADR-018`'s own established practice). Update `prd.md` §14/§15 as each piece of Phase 1 actually ships. Specifically still open, tracked here so none of it is silently lost:
- The droplet itself, Managed MySQL instance, Spaces buckets, Reserved IP, and Cloudflare Origin certificate are none of them provisioned yet — this ADR is the design to provision against once purchasing happens.
- Decision 3's three Redis revisit triggers must be actively checked as the system evolves, not left to be noticed by accident — same "don't let deferred quietly become forgotten" discipline this doc already applies to `ADR-019` decisions 2/3.
- Decision 9's Phase 2 (Playwright E2E) is the explicit next priority once this ADR is settled — do not let it quietly slide indefinitely the way a "someday" item can.
- This ADR is independent of, and does not change, `ADR-019`'s own fix-now list (login rate-limiting, Xendit idempotency key, the `SupplierCircuitBreaker`, etc.) — those remain separately tracked pure-code items with no infra dependency; don't conflate "production host is now decided" with "those are now done."
- Implementation (Dockerfiles, Compose file, GitHub Actions workflow, actual droplet/Managed-DB/Spaces provisioning) is explicitly deferred to a new session, per the founder's own instruction this session.

**Addendum — Phase 1 shipped (Dockerfiles, `docker-compose.prod.yml`, CI), 2026-07-30 (same session, later, per ADR-021 item 3):** everything decision #10 said was buildable without the droplet is now built and locally proven — the SSH-deploy job and the git-remote creation are the only pieces still deferred (see below), exactly as scoped.

**Prerequisite found and fixed first, before any Docker/CI file:** this session's own queue-worker-sizing research (Laravel's official docs, cross-checked against the 8 GiB/4 vCPU droplet spec) confirmed decision #5's `queue-worker-orders`/`queue-worker-pricesync` split was still just a name on paper — no job actually declared a queue. Fixed via `$this->onQueue(...)` in each job's constructor (`FulfillOrderJob`/`ResendOrderDeliveryJob` → `orders`, `SyncSupplierPricesJob` → `price-sync`) — **not** a redeclared `public $queue` property, which PHP rejects as an incompatible redefinition of `Illuminate\Bus\Queueable`'s own property of the same name (a real, reproducible fatal error hit and fixed live, not assumed). Recommended sizing: 2 queues, 1 worker process each for now (zero real traffic today per ADR-021's own framing) — scale `queue-worker-orders` via `docker compose up -d --scale queue-worker-orders=2` once real order volume justifies it, no code change needed to do that.

**Built and locally verified** (`docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml build` + `up`, all before any droplet exists):
- `backend/Dockerfile` — multi-stage (composer deps → vite asset build for the unrelated default `welcome.blade.php` scaffold page → `php-fpm` runtime), reused unmodified by both queue-worker services (only the container `command:` differs).
- `admin/Dockerfile`, `storefront/Dockerfile` — standard Next.js `output: "standalone"` multi-stage build (added to both `next.config.ts` files — neither set this before). `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` (the one env var either app reads) is passed as a Docker build arg, not just an env_file — confirmed this matters: Next.js inlines `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` into the client bundle at build time, a runtime-only env var would silently not apply.
- `backend/docker/nginx/default.conf` + a `nginx` compose service — standard two-container `nginx` + `php-fpm` split (fastcgi_pass over the compose network), not bundled into one image, keeping one-process-per-container. Host-level Nginx (Cloudflare Origin CA/SSL, decision #8) stays out of scope — it needs the real droplet's filesystem to configure, reverse-proxies to this stack's one published port.
- `docker-compose.prod.yml` (repo root) — 7 services (`nginx`, `php-fpm`, `queue-worker-orders`, `queue-worker-price-sync`, `admin`, `storefront`, `redis`), no `mysql`/Spaces service (both off-box per decisions #2/nothing self-hosted). Distinct from, and doesn't touch, `backend/docker-compose.yml` (ADR-010's own local-only file).
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — 4 real jobs (backend sqlite suite, backend concurrency suite against a `mysql:8.4` GitHub Actions service container, `admin`/`storefront` tsc+build+eslint) plus a `build-and-push` job gated on all four, pushing to DigitalOcean Container Registry. **Confirmed, not glossed over:** this last job needs `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN` (repo secret) and an actual DO Container Registry resource, neither provisioned — a real requirement beyond decision #10's "only the SSH-deploy step needs a real target." The SSH-deploy job itself is deliberately not written at all yet (a disabled stub is worse than no job).
- `predis/predis` added to `backend/composer.json` — decision #3 provisions Redis for cache, and there was no PHP Redis client installed at all until now (checked directly, not assumed).

**Two real bugs found and fixed only by actually building and running the stack locally, not by reading the Dockerfile and assuming it works:**
1. `mbstring`'s configure step failed on `php:8.3(/8.4)-fpm-alpine` for a missing `oniguruma-dev` Alpine package — added.
2. **PHP version mismatch:** `composer.json` declares `"php": "^8.3"`, but `composer.lock` — generated against this machine's actual local PHP 8.4.23 — locked at least one dependency to a floor of `>=8.4.1`. `php:8.3-fpm-alpine` failed outright at Composer's own `platform_check.php`. Switched the Dockerfile (and the CI workflow's `setup-php` step) to `8.4`, matching what's actually required. `composer.json`'s own declared constraint is left as-is (not edited this pass, out of this plan's scope) — worth a future one-line correction so it stops claiming `^8.3` when the lock file already requires `^8.4`.
3. **Stale local `bootstrap/cache/{packages,services}.php`** (Laravel's compiled provider-discovery cache, generated locally with dev dependencies present) were being copied into the image by the final stage's `COPY . .`, clobbering whatever `composer dump-autoload --no-dev` had freshly regenerated one stage earlier — surfaced as `Class "Laravel\Pail\PailServiceProvider" not found` (a dev-only package correctly absent from the `--no-dev` image, but still referenced by the stale cache). Fixed by adding `bootstrap/cache/*.php` to `backend/.dockerignore` — the image now regenerates this cache itself from its own (no-dev) `vendor/`, never inherits the host's.

After both fixes: `GET /api/health` through the `nginx`→`php-fpm` stack returned a real, correctly-structured `503 {"status":"degraded","checks":{"database":false,"queue":false}}` — not a crash. This is the *expected* result for this local check (no real `.env`/DB is wired into this verification, by design — production secrets aren't baked into the image or committed), and it directly confirms the mechanism CI's future SSH-deploy rollback step depends on actually works: a broken/unconfigured deploy reports `503`, not a silent `200`.

**Consequence to track:**
- `composer.json`'s `"php": "^8.3"` constraint is stale (should say `^8.4`) — a small, safe follow-up, not done this pass to keep this plan's scope to infra files only.
- Still genuinely not done: the SSH-deploy CI job, the actual droplet/Managed MySQL/Spaces/Reserved IP/Cloudflare Origin cert, the DO Container Registry + its access-token secret, and git-remote creation (ADR-021 item 4) — none of Phase 1's local build/proof work substitutes for any of these.
- **Local-dev regression caught and fixed same session, not left for a future session to discover as a "stuck job" mystery:** now that all 3 jobs declare a real queue name (`orders`/`price-sync`, not the implicit `default`), `composer run dev`'s own `queue:listen` call (previously no `--queue=` flag, which per `WorkCommand::getQueue()`'s own source falls back to the connection's configured default queue) would have silently stopped processing every one of them. Fixed in the same pass: `backend/composer.json`'s `dev` script now runs `queue:listen --queue=orders,price-sync ...`. `docs/prd.md`'s own "known gotchas" note (queue-worker-not-running) updated to match — any other manual `queue:work`/`queue:listen` invocation (e.g. alongside Herd) must include the same `--queue=orders,price-sync` or it processes nothing.

**Investigation notes (reference only, not part of the Decision above) — capacity analysis against real order history, 2026-08-14 (discussion only, nothing provisioned/changed).** Founder supplied `docs/orders.csv` — the current live topup site's real order export, 28,848 rows, 2025-12-28 to 2026-08-14 (230 days) — to sanity-check whether Decision 1's droplet (8 GiB/4 vCPU) and Decision 2's Managed MySQL tier (2 GiB/1 vCPU) can actually carry this business's real transaction shape, not just a guessed one. Findings, derived by direct analysis of the CSV (not assumed):

- **Volume:** ~125 orders/day average (~4,008/month over full months), confirming the founder's own recollection of ~RM100k–200k/month (paid-only monthly revenue ranged RM66.5k–244k across Jan–Jul 2026, avg RM136.6k, avg order value RM43.78).
- **Burst is very light relative to the chosen compute:** busiest single minute ever recorded was 9 orders; busiest 5-minute window was 28 orders (~0.09 orders/sec); the highest number of orders sharing the exact same second, across the entire 230-day history, was 3. This is nowhere near saturating a single php-fpm worker pool on a 4 vCPU box, even accounting for `CheckoutController::store()`'s synchronous payment-gateway call (fulfillment itself is already queued, per Decision on ADR-014).
- **Linear extrapolation to 5x/10x/20x today's volume** (RM1–2 million/month lands around x7–x15 of the current ~RM136.6k/month baseline) still projects peak concurrency in the tens of orders/minute, single digits/sec sustained — comfortably within Decision 1's droplet, with the explicit caveat that this is a **linear scaling of today's organic pattern**, not a model of sharper, campaign-driven bursts a real 10–20x growth push might actually produce; a genuine flash-sale-shaped spike could cluster far more tightly than this extrapolation assumes.
- **Managed MySQL connection ceiling checked directly against DigitalOcean's own published limits** (`docs.digitalocean.com/products/databases/mysql/details/limits/`): Decision 2's chosen 2 GiB/1 vCPU tier allows **150 backend connections** (1 GiB → 75, 4 GiB → 400, 8 GiB → 800). Estimated worst-case concurrent connection demand at 10–20x volume (~30–50 php-fpm workers plus the `orders`/`price-sync` queue workers plus the 15-minute reconciliation commands) sits well under that ceiling — connection *count* is not expected to be the constraint even at 20x.
- **Genuinely still unverified, not resolvable from documentation or the CSV alone — needs a real load test once the droplet/DB actually exist:** sustained write-throughput/IOPS under real concurrent load, actual droplet↔Managed-MySQL network latency, and `pm.max_children`/queue-worker-count tuning (none of this is configured yet — Phase 1 only proved the images build and run, not real production concurrency).
- **One risk this analysis surfaced is independent of order volume entirely, present even at 1x:** Decision 1's single-droplet/single-region choice remains this ADR's own explicitly named revisit trigger (sustained high CPU/RAM, or a confirmed second-country launch) — a serious growth push toward the RM1–2m/month range is a reasonable point to re-open that trigger deliberately, not because compute runs out, but because a single box stays a single point of failure regardless of how much headroom it has.

**Consequence to track:** no infrastructure decision changed by this analysis — Decision 1 (droplet size) and Decision 2 (Managed MySQL tier) both hold up against real historical data through the 10–20x range discussed. Revisit this addendum at the start of the actual deployment session (Decision 10's "build sequencing" — droplet/Managed MySQL not yet purchased) to decide, with real numbers from a load test, whether either tier needs adjusting before go-live, and to weigh whether the redundancy trigger above is worth acting on proactively given the founder's stated growth target.

**Investigation notes (reference only, not part of the Decision above) — availability-under-load and detection/alerting discussion, 2026-08-14 (same day, discussion only, nothing built/changed).** Founder asked two related questions ahead of the deployment session: (1) under heavy request load, can the site actually go down; (2) as a non-technical ("vibe coder") operator, how would a problem or an attack attempt even be noticed. Both answered against what's actually decided/built today, not assumed:

1. **Availability under load — real, accepted risk, not a new gap.** What already protects: Cloudflare Proxy in front of the droplet (Decision 8, absorbs volumetric DDoS at the edge before it reaches the box), per-route rate limiting (`throttle:10,1` checkout, `5,1` login, `120,1` on both webhook routes — `ADR-014`/foundation-security.md §5), the Cloud Firewall's minimal 80/443/22 surface (Decision 7), and the per-supplier circuit breaker (keeps a down Gamevion from cascading into the whole delivery queue). What does **not** protect, by deliberate, already-recorded design: Decision 1's single-droplet/single-region choice — no load balancer, no auto-scaling. Organic growth, including the 10–20x range in the capacity addendum above, stays within the droplet's headroom. A genuine sustained L7 flood or an extreme, attack-shaped spike is a different failure mode from organic burst and is **not** fully covered by today's design — this is Decision 1's own named revisit trigger, not a newly discovered hole.
2. **Detection/alerting for a non-technical operator — a real, currently-open gap.** `ADR-014` decision #6 explicitly declined external error-tracking (Sentry etc., cost/data-residency, before real production traffic existed) — that reasoning was sound at the time but was never revisited against an actual imminent deployment. Today: `GET /api/health` exists but nothing polls it; admin login attempts are logged (`prd.md`'s 2026-07-29 entry) but nothing alerts on a suspicious pattern; the blacklist/velocity guard blocks known-bad actors automatically but is reactive (an admin must add the entry after noticing); admin MFA remains descoped (`foundation-security.md` §1). A founder without deep security background has, today, no push notification of either an outage or a suspicious pattern — only a manual SSH-and-read-the-log path.

**Consequence to track — concrete, low-effort items to decide (not silently re-defer) at the actual deployment session, none requiring new application code:**
- An external uptime monitor (e.g. UptimeRobot/Better Uptime free tier) polling `GET /api/health`, notifying by email/SMS/WhatsApp on failure — closes the "nobody is watching health-check" gap directly.
- DigitalOcean's built-in droplet monitoring + alert policies (CPU/RAM/disk thresholds) — free, a checkbox at provisioning time, not built yet.
- Review Cloudflare's dashboard security settings once the domain is live (manual "Under Attack Mode" toggle, managed WAF rules on the free tier) — not yet configured, since there's no live domain to configure it against.
- **Re-open `ADR-014` decision #6's Sentry/error-tracking deferral deliberately**, now that a real deployment is imminent rather than hypothetical — its original justification ("before real production traffic exists") is the exact condition about to change, and this ADR's own governing priority (Decision statement: "money spent to keep the system from crashing... is money the founder is willing to spend") plausibly extends to observability, not just compute/DB tier.
- Reconsider admin MFA (`foundation-security.md` §1, AUTH-7) given it's the single-factor weak point on the two account types (withdrawal approval, blacklist management) with the most damage potential if compromised — still a founder call to make, not decided here.
